1.pericope_label: Behold, the day of the Lord cometh, and thy spoil shall be divided in the midst of thee. For I will gather all nations against Jerusalem to battle; and the city shall be taken, and the houses rifled, and the women ravished; and half of the city shall go forth into captivity, and the residue of the people shall not be cut off from the city. Then shall the Lord go forth, and fight against those nations, as when he fought in the day of battle.

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the opening as a day coming for the Lord on which he will manifest his glory, and rather than decide whether the Roman capture answers to the prophecy sets a long passage of the historian before his readers and asks what room it leaves for a remnant; Keil and Delitzsch reach the same rendering and set out the structure, the day first bringing calamity and that calamity occasioning the display of divine might.

Gill denies the Roman reference on the ground that they were not all nations and that the whole city went captive with none remaining, preferring the last battle or a future dispossession; Calvin sets aside the readings that make the chapter concern Antichrist, the last day, or the Roman destruction, and holds that the calamities then at hand are meant, his purpose being to prepare the returned exiles for trials.

Clarke refers the opening to the Roman destruction and the sequel to the extermination of the enemies of Christianity, notes that many were preserved for slavery and the provincial theatres, and admits the verse about the Lord going forth is obscure; Wesley likewise names the Romans and identifies the residue as those spared by the conqueror.

Henry keeps the Roman reference but makes the alternation the point, God's providences towards his church strangely changing, and reads the remnant as mercy, judgment beginning at the house of God but neither ending there nor making a full end.

debates.question: What event does the chapter describe?

positions.position: The Roman destruction of Jerusalem, the prophet then passing to the latter days.
Not the Romans, who were not all nations and left none remaining; rather the last battle, or a future dispossession after the Jews reinhabit the city.
Neither Antichrist nor the last day nor the Roman destruction, but the calamities close at hand when the city was not yet built.
Left open: the historian's account of the capture is set out and the reader asked what room it leaves for a remnant.

debates.question: How should the opening phrase be rendered?

positions.position: A day cometh for the Lord, on which he will signally manifest his glory.
The day of vengeance, coming upon a sinful and unthankful people.

outliers.claim: Rejects all three current readings of the chapter and holds that the prophet meant the calamities immediately at hand, since the city had not yet been built and evils continued from the rebuilding until the coming of Christ, his purpose being pastoral, that the returned exiles might be prepared for trials and not repent of returning.

themes: Behold, the day of the Lord cometh, and thy spoil shall be divided in the midst of thee.

For I will gather all nations against Jerusalem to battle; and the city shall be taken, and the houses rifled, and the women ravished; and half of the city shall go forth into captivity, and the residue of the people shall not be cut off from the city.
Then shall the Lord go forth, and fight against those nations, as when he fought in the day of battle.

4.pericope_label: And his feet shall stand in that day upon the mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east, and the mount of Olives shall cleave in the midst thereof toward the east and toward the west, and there shall be a very great valley; and half of the mountain shall remove toward the north, and half of it toward the south. And ye shall flee to the valley of the mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach unto Azal: yea, ye shall flee, like as ye fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah: and the Lord my God shall come, and all the saints with thee. And it shall come to pass in that day, that the light shall not be clear, nor dark: But it shall be one day which shall be known to the Lord, not day, nor night: but it shall come to pass, that at evening time it shall be light.

schools.summary: Ellicott says the language is of course figurative, rejects a modern rendering of the flight as unsupported and an ancient revocalisation as inappropriate, argues at length that the earthquake used as a date does not fix the prophecy to that reign, would read angels for saints, and re-renders the strange light as no light with the heavenly bodies failing; Keil and Delitzsch translate to the same effect.

Gill argues that the standing of the feet cannot refer to the destruction of the city, since no such appearance occurred then, and takes it of a future descent to the very spot of the ascension, reporting also a Jewish notion about the rolling of the dead.

Clarke gives both a conqueror's appearing and the Roman siege, commits to the second, and suggests the removing of half the mountain means the lines of circumvallation; Wesley reads the light as judgment mixed with mercy and the day as one continued day with no setting sun.

debates.question: What is the cleaving of the mountain?

positions.position: A future miraculous descent, the return being to the spot from which the ascension took place.
The entrenchments and lines of circumvallation cut on that mountain during the Roman siege.
Figurative language: an earthquake commonly accompanies the Lord's appearing.

debates.question: What is the light that is neither clear nor dark?

positions.position: A mixture of justice and mercy, with more light than darkness since mercy triumphs over judgment.
Not a mixture at all: there shall be no light and the heavenly bodies shall fail, a murky gloom like a desert sand-storm.

outliers.claim: Argues that the earthquake used as a date does not fix the prophecy to that reign, since the event left so deep an impression that it became an era to reckon from, that the second person need not address the hearers directly given a nation's continuity, and that the appended royal title might imply hearers needed reminding who the king was.

themes: And his feet shall stand in that day upon the mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east, and the mount of Olives shall cleave in the midst thereof toward the east and toward the west, and there shall be a very great valley; and half of the mountain shall remove toward the north, and half of it toward the south.

And ye shall flee to the valley of the mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach unto Azal: yea, ye shall flee, like as ye fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah: and the Lord my God shall come, and all the saints with thee.
And it shall come to pass in that day, that the light shall not be clear, nor dark:
But it shall be one day which shall be known to the Lord, not day, nor night: but it shall come to pass, that at evening time it shall be light.

8.pericope_label: And it shall be in that day, that living waters shall go out from Jerusalem; half of them toward the former sea, and half of them toward the hinder sea: in summer and in winter shall it be. And the Lord shall be king over all the earth: in that day shall there be one Lord, and his name one. All the land shall be turned as a plain from Geba to Rimmon south of Jerusalem: and it shall be lifted up, and inhabited in her place, from Benjamin’s gate unto the place of the first gate, unto the corner gate, and from the tower of Hananeel unto the king’s winepresses. And men shall dwell in it, and there shall be no more utter destruction; but Jerusalem shall be safely inhabited.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the living waters as the symbol of divine knowledge, identifies the two seas as the boundaries of the whole land, holds that the context allows only the narrower sense of all the land while conceding that the words may have a wider application than the prophet contemplated, and gives a long topographical account of the two boundary places and the four city landmarks; Keil and Delitzsch supply the renderings.

Gill develops the figure of the living waters at length and takes the kingship of the spiritual reign, with churches everywhere and every kind of nation becoming Christian, and reads the levelling as the encircling mountains made a plain so the city may be seen.

Clarke turns the waters into a route of diffusion, renders the levelling as God encompassing the whole land as a plain and casting his defence around it, and says there shall be only one religion whose essence is the two great commandments; Wesley reads the levelling agriculturally and then morally.

Henry dates the springing of the living waters to the outpouring of the Spirit on the apostles, and observes that where the gospel goes with the graces of the Spirit the country is watered as well as the city.

debates.question: Does the kingship extend over all the earth or all the land?

positions.position: Over all the earth: churches set up everywhere and every kind of nation becoming Christian.
The context allows only all the land, though the words may have a wider application than the prophet ever contemplated.

debates.question: How should the levelling of the land be rendered?

positions.position: The whole land turned as the great rift plain, the lifting up of the city being figurative of its religious prominence.
Rather, God shall encompass the whole land as a plain, casting his defence around it.
The encircling mountains made a plain so that the city may be seen.
Uneven and rocky ground changed into fruitful vineyards, figuring a fruitful and humble church.

outliers.claim: Observes that the name the city bears today, meaning the holy place, is itself a testimony to the prophecy, since the nations in adopting the appellation from the Jews acknowledge the city to have been the fountain-head of religious knowledge.

themes: And it shall be in that day, that living waters shall go out from Jerusalem; half of them toward the former sea, and half of them toward the hinder sea: in summer and in winter shall it be.
And the Lord shall be king over all the earth: in that day shall there be one Lord, and his name one.

All the land shall be turned as a plain from Geba to Rimmon south of Jerusalem: and it shall be lifted up, and inhabited in her place, from Benjamin’s gate unto the place of the first gate, unto the corner gate, and from the tower of Hananeel unto the king’s winepresses.
And men shall dwell in it, and there shall be no more utter destruction; but Jerusalem shall be safely inhabited.

12.pericope_label: And this shall be the plague wherewith the Lord will smite all the people that have fought against Jerusalem; Their flesh shall consume away while they stand upon their feet, and their eyes shall consume away in their holes, and their tongue shall consume away in their mouth. And it shall come to pass in that day, that a great tumult from the Lord shall be among them; and they shall lay hold every one on the hand of his neighbour, and his hand shall rise up against the hand of his neighbour. And Judah also shall fight at Jerusalem; and the wealth of all the heathen round about shall be gathered together, gold, and silver, and apparel, in great abundance. And so shall be the plague of the horse, of the mule, of the camel, and of the ass, and of all the beasts that shall be in these tents, as this plague.

schools.summary: Ellicott gives a military and psychological account of the fighting, the whole people taking courage from the panic of a terror-driven and plague-stricken foe, justifies the spoil by the practice of eastern armies marching with valuables, and compares the destruction of the beasts to that of a man who took forbidden spoil; Keil and Delitzsch supply the wording of the tumult without interpretation.

Gill applies the plague to the antichristian states and identifies it with the seven plagues of a later vision, and takes the combatants for the armies of heaven who follow the Lamb against the antichristian princes.

Clarke reads the plague plainly as the effects of famine and compares the visitation on the animals to the cattle and goods struck in Egypt; Wesley explains the tumult as murmurs running into civil war, keeps the fighters historical and suggests a Maccabean leader may be meant.

positions.position: The professing people of Christ, the armies of heaven who follow the Lamb.
The Jews, and possibly a Maccabean leader is intended.
The whole people, both those escaped from the city and those outside the walls, taking courage from the enemy's panic.

debates.question: What is the plague that falls on the besiegers?

positions.position: One or more of the seven plagues to be inflicted on the antichristian states.
The effects of famine, all the enemies being destroyed.
A tumult from the Lord in which each turns on his neighbour, so that they destroy themselves.

outliers.claim: Justifies the wealth gathered by an appeal to military practice, that oriental armies always march with quantities of gold, silver and other valuables, citing both a scriptural instance and a much later one from the campaigns of an Indian emperor.

themes: And this shall be the plague wherewith the Lord will smite all the people that have fought against Jerusalem; Their flesh shall consume away while they stand upon their feet, and their eyes shall consume away in their holes, and their tongue shall consume away in their mouth.

And it shall come to pass in that day, that a great tumult from the Lord shall be among them; and they shall lay hold every one on the hand of his neighbour, and his hand shall rise up against the hand of his neighbour.
And Judah also shall fight at Jerusalem; and the wealth of all the heathen round about shall be gathered together, gold, and silver, and apparel, in great abundance.
And so shall be the plague of the horse, of the mule, of the camel, and of the ass, and of all the beasts that shall be in these tents, as this plague.

16.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass, that every one that is left of all the nations which came against Jerusalem shall even go up from year to year to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, and to keep the feast of tabernacles. And it shall be, that whoso will not come up of all the families of the earth unto Jerusalem to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, even upon them shall be no rain. And if the family of Egypt go not up, and come not, that have no rain; there shall be the plague, wherewith the Lord will smite the heathen that come not up to keep the feast of tabernacles. This shall be the punishment of Egypt, and the punishment of all nations that come not up to keep the feast of tabernacles.

schools.summary: Ellicott explains the choice of the feast by its character as the thanksgiving for harvest and vintage on which the Lord is praised as the God of nature, insists the prophecy is not to be taken literally, calls the received rendering of one clause impossible and offers two repairs, and argues from the geography of the Nile that the withholding of rain cannot be literal; Keil and Delitzsch head the section as the conversion of the heathen.
Gill insists the threat of withheld rain belongs to times preceding the spiritual reign, takes the family of Egypt for the Papists, and notes that the word rendered punishment is in the original sin.

Clarke explains the choice of the feast by what it commemorated and refers it to the final restoration after long wandering in vice and error, reads the withheld rain as a rule about neglected ordinances, and refers the family of Egypt to Jews who fled persecution and built a temple there; Wesley takes one festival by a figure for all days consecrated to worship.
Henry works out what the conversion involves, former enemies becoming as much the city's admirers as they had been her adversaries, and distinguishes foes made a footstool from foes made friends.

debates.question: Why is the feast of tabernacles named?

positions.position: Because it commemorated the forty years of wandering, and so marks a restoration after long wandering in vice and error.
Because it is the thanksgiving for harvest and vintage, on which the Lord is especially praised as the beneficent God of nature.
One solemn festival is put by a figure for all days consecrated to holy worship.

debates.question: Who is the family of Egypt?

positions.position: The Papists, so called for their tyranny and idolatry.
Jews who fled persecution, settled in Egypt and built a temple there.
The clause cannot be read literally at all, since Egypt can only lack water when the lands to its south do.

outliers.claim: Argues from the hydrology of the Nile that the prophecy cannot be literal: if Egypt were punished by deficiency of water, the country upriver would suffer at the same time even though its people attended the feast, since Egypt can only lack water in connection with the lands to its south.

themes: And it shall come to pass, that every one that is left of all the nations which came against Jerusalem shall even go up from year to year to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, and to keep the feast of tabernacles.
And it shall be, that whoso will not come up of all the families of the earth unto Jerusalem to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, even upon them shall be no rain.
And if the family of Egypt go not up, and come not, that have no rain; there shall be the plague, wherewith the Lord will smite the heathen that come not up to keep the feast of tabernacles.
This shall be the punishment of Egypt, and the punishment of all nations that come not up to keep the feast of tabernacles.

20.pericope_label: In that day shall there be upon the bells of the horses, HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD; and the pots in the Lord’s house shall be like the bowls before the altar. Yea, every pot in Jerusalem and in Judah shall be holiness unto the Lord of hosts: and all they that sacrifice shall come and take of them, and seethe therein: and in that day there shall be no more the Canaanite in the house of the Lord of hosts.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the Canaanite of the closing clause as denoting an alien or unbeliever, and conveys its force by comparing how certain national and religious names function as insults among his own contemporaries; Keil and Delitzsch give the final verse without comment.

Gill dates the whole to a new state of things after the destruction of the antichristian party, and explains the sanctifying of every pot by the number of sacrifices, the vessels of the house being insufficient.

Clarke describes the bells actually hung on beasts in the East from paintings before him, states the principle that a man's labour and even his animals and instruments are consecrated, identifies the Canaanite as the merchant, and applies the clause to collections taken in his own churches; Wesley draws the gradation between the kitchen pots and the bowls that received the blood, so that the holiness of those days exceeds the former.

debates.question: Who is the Canaanite in the house of the Lord?

positions.position: The merchant: where such are tolerated in a place dedicated to divine worship it is not the house of the Lord of hosts.
Any of the accursed nation, or one who makes merchandise of religion.
An alien or unbeliever, the word carrying the force of a national insult.

debates.question: What is the point of comparing the pots with the bowls?

positions.position: The meanest utensil shall be as the vessels of silver and gold used in solemn sacrifice.
The kitchen pots were less sacred than the bowls that received the blood, so the holiness of those days shall exceed the holiness of the former.
The sacrifices will be so numerous that the vessels of the house will not suffice, so every pot in city and country must be sanctified.

outliers.claim: Describes from Asiatic paintings before him the little bells tied to the legs and the larger ones about the necks of horses, mules and camels, particularly in a picture of a caravan passing through a valley of serpents on an eastern island, and notes that the margin reads bridles rather than bells.

themes: In that day shall there be upon the bells of the horses, HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD; and the pots in the Lord’s house shall be like the bowls before the altar.

Yea, every pot in Jerusalem and in Judah shall be holiness unto the Lord of hosts: and all they that sacrifice shall come and take of them, and seethe therein: and in that day there shall be no more the Canaanite in the house of the Lord of hosts.
